---
title: "Representation learning and efficient perceptual encoding"
description: >-
  Which distinctions a perceptual encoder retains and how a learned prior
  controls their coding cost.
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- An encoder must preserve distinctions useful for decisions, not merely
  produce latents that are easy to predict.
- In the primary aesthetics model, the encoder can learn; its parameters and
  the work policy parameters are frozen only during the update of the perceptual
  prior.
- Temporal prediction and sensory reconstruction are candidate training signals.
  Neither avoiding collapse nor achieving a good variational objective
  guarantees task relevance.
- We propose that an organism uses $\mathcal C$ to estimate the minimum
  realizable cost of communicating what its latents convey about sensory input.
  A mismatched prior overestimates that minimum; a matched prior gives the
  mutual information $I(X;Z)$ exactly.
:::

In [reinforcement learning under partial observability](pomdp-rl.qmd), the
encoder $F(z\mid x)$ determines which distinctions in the sensory input $x$
reach the policy as a latent $z$. If two observations call for different actions
given the same memory, mapping both to the same latent distribution leaves the
policy unable to respond differently. Conversely, preserving every sensory
detail can expend limited capacity on distinctions that never affect a decision.

## Learning by temporal prediction

The predictive learning rule studied by @halvagal2023 works in latent space,
without reconstructing the sensory input. Predictive plasticity brings
representations of temporally adjacent inputs together, supporting invariance;
Hebbian plasticity preserves variation in activity and counters collapse.
Variation alone does not tell us whether the encoder distinguishes situations
that require different actions.

## Learning by reconstruction

A variational autoencoder adds a decoder $p_\psi(x\mid z)$. On inputs sampled
from the attended-input distribution $p_{\mathrm{att}}$, let expectations be
under $p_{\mathrm{att}}(x)F(z\mid x)$. Following @alemi2018 [Eqs. 2--6], define
reconstruction distortion and coding cost by

$$
\mathcal D = \mathbb E[-\log p_\psi(X\mid Z)],\qquad
\mathcal C = \mathbb E\!\left[\log\frac{F(Z\mid X)}{R_\theta(Z)}\right],
$$ {#eq-distortion-coding-cost}

where $R_\theta$ is a normalized latent prior. Jointly minimizing
$\mathcal D+\beta\mathcal C$ over encoder, decoder, and prior trades
reconstruction fidelity against coding cost for $\beta\geq0$; at $\beta=1$
the objective is the expected negative ELBO. The likelihood determines which
errors matter: a fixed-variance isotropic Gaussian gives squared error up to a
scale factor and a constant.

With well-defined entropy and log-loss, $H(X)-\mathcal D\leq I(X;Z)$.
Beating the best input-independent reconstruction loss therefore requires
informative latents. A good ELBO alone does not: an expressive decoder can
ignore $Z$, and positive coding cost can reflect prior mismatch rather than
retained information. Evaluate rate and distortion separately, then test whether
the policy can actually use the retained information on its task.

## Efficient encoding with a perceptual prior {#efficient-encoding}

Transmitting a perceptual distinction to the circuits that use it consumes
physical resources. The biological hypothesis is that $\mathcal C$ approximates
the minimum realizable cost of conveying what the latent represents about the
input.

To see why the prior matters for this estimate, let $q_F(z)$ be the
frequency (or density) of latent $z$ when inputs come from $p_{\mathrm{att}}$
and are encoded by $F$. The coding cost above decomposes as [@alemi2018]
$$
\mathcal C
= I(X;Z) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_F\Vert R_\theta\right).
$$ {#eq-coding-cost-decomposition}
For a fixed encoder and input distribution, $I(X;Z)$ is the minimum over
all priors: the mismatch term is nonnegative and vanishes when $R_\theta=q_F$.
Fitting the prior therefore tightens the estimate from above without changing
the minimum. For discrete latents at that minimum,
$\mathcal C=H(Z)-H(Z\mid X)$. Subtracting the conditional entropy matters.
If the encoder outputs a fair coin flip independently of the input, specifying
the outcome takes one bit, but it conveys no information about the input.
With a matched prior, $\mathcal C$ is therefore zero.

When **training the encoder**, penalizing $\mathcal C$ trades the benefit of
preserving a distinction against its estimated communication cost. Although
$\mathcal C$ bounds retained information from above, its role here is to price
that cost. A distortion or task objective must still specify what
is worth keeping; a constant latent would be cheap but uninformative. When
**training only the prior**, with the encoder and input distribution fixed,
neither the representations nor $I(X;Z)$ change. Minimizing expected latent
negative log-likelihood then minimizes only the mismatch term, which vanishes if
$R_\theta=q_F$. The [binary rate–distortion example](rate-distortion-prior.qmd)
shows the coding bound falling while reconstruction error stays fixed.

## Connection to aesthetic preferences

Either approach could supply an encoder for the
[computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd). In its
primary model, the encoder and the task (work) policy are frozen only during
the network optimization phase, when the perceptual prior is updated. The prior
thus has a stable target for that update, but the latent distribution it must
predict can change as the encoder or work policy learns between updates. Which
training stimuli, likelihood, architecture, and compression weight preserve
useful distinctions remains an empirical question.
